message.content:
For two positive integers \(a\) and \(b\), their product \(ab\) is a perfect square exactly when \(a\) and \(b\) have the same squarefree part.

So group the numbers \(1,2,\dots,16\) by their squarefree part:

\[
\begin{aligned}
1 &: \{1,4,9,16\}\\
2 &: \{2,8\}\\
3 &: \{3,12\}\\
5 &: \{5\}\\
6 &: \{6\}\\
7 &: \{7\}\\
10 &: \{10\}\\
11 &: \{11\}\\
13 &: \{13\}\\
14 &: \{14\}\\
15 &: \{15\}
\end{aligned}
\]

There are \(11\) groups. Within any one group, any two numbers have a product that is a perfect square. Therefore, to avoid such a product, Jillian can draw at most one number from each group.

She can achieve this maximum by drawing one number from each of the \(11\) groups. For example, draw

\[
1,2,3,5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15.
\]

No two of these have the same squarefree part, so no product is a perfect square.

Thus the maximum number of slips she can draw without obtaining a product that is a perfect square is

\[
\boxed{11}
\]

The answer is 11.
